Before the bill is disposed
of, Mr. Chairman, I desire to give to the farming communities of the province of Quebec a clear understanding of subsection (9) of section 6. I was called out of the house for a few minutes and while absent it was disposed of by the committee. Before this bill was submitted to the committee I had a motion on the order paper-as had also the member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Girouard)-that all persons engaged in tillage of the soil be exempt from the bankruptcy law. I put that motion on the order paper-and I have no doubt the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska did so for the same reason-because I had received several resolutions in its favour from farmers' clubs and other farmers' organizations. I think I can speak for every member of the committee when I say all political ideas were forgotten for the time being when this section came before the committee and only the welfare of the farming class was considered. Not one representation was made before the committee against the change made in the bankruptcy law by subsection (9) of section 6. Since then unfortunately more or less division seems to have arisen, even among farmers, with regard to this change, and I hold in my hand a couple of newspapers containing articles claiming that the remedy will be worse than the disease. Therefore I desire to make it plain that the committee inserted subsection (9) in response to what we considered was a unanimous demand made in the interests of the farming class of the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to endorse what my hon. friend has said, and,

Bankruptcy Act
as a member of the committee, to speak in defence of this bill, which to-day has met some rather strong criticism. The bankruptcy law has never been very popular. From its inception the act has been criticized, especially in the province from which I come, but I think the criticism was not limited to Quebec. In 1923 when Sir Lomer Gouin was Minister of Justice he was instrumental in amending the act by inserting some special provisions to make it more in harmony with the civil law of the province of Quebec. Those amendments have to some extent alleviated the objections that existed against the law, but not completely. More particularly was there strong criticism of the farming community being subjected to the bankruptcy law. Of course, it has always been claimed that it was a privilege for the farmers, and even during this session when our committee was sitting members from the other provinces could not very well understand why the farmers of Quebec should ask to be removed from t)he operation of the act. They thought it was a privilege for the farmers to be able to get a discharge from their debts and start anew. But of course conditions among the farming communities in Quebec are not similar to those among the farmers in the other provinces, and it has been clearly demonstrated to the satisfaction even of my colleagues from the other provinces that the act instead of helping the farmers of Quebec has worked an injury to their credit. The farmers of Quebec do not borrow money from the banks or trust companies; they usually borrow from other farmers in their own village or their own parish. These loans are based on mutual confidence, and unfortunately the fact that many farmers were induced to make assignments has taken away some of the confidence that formerly prevailed in the farming communities, which has been rather prejudicial to the farmers in the course of their business operations. The Minister of Agriculture, the presidents of agricultural associations and many other persons have represented that it was better for the farmers [DOT]of Quebec that they should be removed from the operation of the act, and in that respect the committee has been unanimous. If it were for that provision pnly, I think hon. members from the province of Quebec should welcome this bill, which is certainly a great improvement and which has been requested for many years.
The other part of the bill, which I have always favoured, is that establishing control. It could not be done otherwise than by having a superintendent of bankruptcy able to supervise the operations of the act. There is no doubt that there have been grave abuses; what has been said to-day by various hon. members shows the need for some control, which could not be maintained except by having a special officer of the government appointed for that purpose and by having the trustees who may be appointed to wind up estates licensed, so that there may be some control in that respect also. We have had many instances of abuses; people have employed agents to canvass the creditors in order to secure their proxies for the purpose of making some money out of the estate, which should go to the creditors. We must not forget, too, that after all assignments, whether voluntary or compulsory, are made on the principle, which is recognized by the law, that they are for the benefit of the creditors, and the creditors should be considered in providing proper machinery for (he administration of the estate.
On the whole I agree with the Minister of Justice that this improved act should be given a trial. If there is the need for further amendment or revision this parliament will be able to deal with it.

May I be allowed to add just a few words. My motion a few weeks ago called for salaried men as well as farmers to be exempted from the operations of the Bankruptcy Act. Personally I should like to have seen that provision included, but the committee felt that since no representation had been made by the salaried class it was inadvisable to take that step. I do believe, however, that there is no more reason why the salaried man should be permitted to make an assignment than there is for the farmer to be allowed to do so. I think it would have been more in the interests of the salaried men if they had been exempted from the privilege of making an assignment. Certainly when a merchant makes an advance to a salaried man he must consider the fact that the next day this man may go to some city and make an assignment of all his assets, if he has any.
I should like to see the exemption extended to all non-traders, which in my opinion would make the law much broader. I do not think it is proper that professional men, for instance, should have the right to make an assignment of their property. I do not think it is in accord with the dignity of the legal profession that lawyers should be allowed to assign all their assets. But, as I said a moment ago, the committee considered that since no representations had been made along
Bankruptcy Act

these lines, no action should be taken. As the ex-Minister of Justice has just said, if the law proves to be satisfactory so much the better, while if in the near future the necessity for these changes becomes apparent, perhaps these other classes of people might be exempted as well as the farmers.
May I ask the government if they have considered the advisability of enlarging the principle established in section 6 by doing away entirely with voluntary assignments?
They have been done away with.
I mean not only for the farmers but for everyone restricting the act only to petitions in bankruptcy.
That question did not come before the committee; no one was desirous of being denied the right to go into bankruptcy in a cheaper, more effective and more expeditious way.

Then I wish to urge upon the government the study of this angle of the question. It means to me that the principle of voluntary assignments is wrong. The desirability of going into bankruptcy should not be left with the debtor; it should rest with his creditors. After all, at the moment of bankruptcy the creditors are the people most concerned in the estate of the debtor, and if you allow the debtor to make a voluntary assignment very often he takes advantage of that privilege in order to defraud his creditors and save what he can from the wreck. This has been done very often; it has come to the notice of lawyers in many cases. If the privilege of voluntary assignment was taken away you would do away with the bankruptcy canvassing racket which has been mentioned during this debate. It seems to me that the initiative should rest with the creditors, who are the people most concerned. At the moment of bankruptcy everything that belongs to the debtor is the common pledge of his creditors, and it should be left to them to say whether or not a particular trader should go into bankruptcy. The trader himself should not have the privilege of going alone, on his own initiative, and making an assignment to the trustee. Therefore I urge the study of this aspect of the question.

We know that the eastern townships at the last election returned mostly supporters of the government of the day, and I suppose that this is one of the plums which the administration is handing over to the eastern townships for the support then given them. But I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that it is to the great disadvantage of the people of the district of Quebec and the people I have the honour to represent in this house. For these reasons I emphatically and strongly protest against the transfer of the activities that were being carried on at that farm to a farm in another district which is much more difficult of access to all the villages in the district of Quebec and on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. While I do not object to this change inuring to the benefit of the people of the eastern townships, I say it is not fair that the activities of this farm, which has been maintained in operation from 1909 until today, under two or three different administrations should be curtailed. My hon. friend from Compton has mentioned the fact that the soil was not suitable. If that is so, the officials of the department who year after year have been advising the minister of agriculture in different governments ought to be criticized because it took them such a long time to find out that the soil was not suitable for experiments. As I say, these activities have been carried on there since 1909 and there was no question at all of changing to any other district. Therefore I think I must be right in saying that this change is a reward which the
government is giving to the eastern townships for the support which it gave the administration in the last election. The government is taking away from the district which I have the honour to represent the advantages which the farmers there received from the activities of this farm and is handing them over to friends of hon. gentlemen opposite.

In reply to what the hon. gentleman has stated, there are no activities being transferred. The work is now being done and has been done at the two experimental farms at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere and Lennoxville. So far as the political significance which the hon. gentleman tried to hitch on to this matter is concerned, that is pretty well answered by the fact that the farm where the cut has been made is situated in the constituency of the Solicitor General, so we cannot very well be accused of any political activity in making this cut. The criticism that was made was not so much with reference to the unsuitability of the soil, as that the soil was not typical of any great area. In addition there is a provincial farm just about twenty-five miles away from this farm at Cap Rouge, and the results of any experiments carried out at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere or at Lennoxville can be demonstrated at Cap Rouge, where there is still remaining the superintendent and the technical adviser to explain any experiments for the benefit of farmers who visit the farm.

In view of the fact that
the experimental farm at Cap Rouge is situated in the constituency of my friend the Solicitor General I should like to say a few words. I am rather surprised that the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay is protesting on account of the fact that there will be greater activity at the experimental farm at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere. I understand that the county of Charlevoix is exactly opposite the county of Kamouraska, and it is easier for the people around St. Irenee or Murray Bay to go to Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, some nine miles away, than to go to Cap Rouge.

Yes, if you would put
on a ferry boat.

I know that my hon.
friend, who is an excellent lawyer, is pleading the case which the former Minister of Justice handed over to him just before he left the chamber. I wish to say on behalf of the electors of Quebec West, who are represented in this house by my friend the Solicitor General, that I have seen the Minister of
Supply-Agriculture

Agriculture and begged him not to curtail too much the activities of that farm, but the Minister of Agriculture pointed out to me, and with justice, that the province of Quebec has always been fairly treated in the matter of experimental farms, that there are five in the province now, and that no other province has been more generously treated. The minister has also been good enough to assure me that the number of experimental farms in the province of Quebec will not be curtailed. I am not an expert in agriculture, but I can quite understand that it might be advisable to transfer activities from one district to another that was more suitable for the purpose. At all events, I do not think we ought to raise any party prejudice in connection with this matter, and we should not try to make the people of the province of Quebec feel that they are being discriminated against. Personally, although I am not an expert, I think that the soil in the county of Kamour-aska and in the district of Lac St. John and Chicoutimi is much more suitable than the soil at Cap Rouge. For these reasons I believe that the Minister of Agriculture is doing no injustice to the province of Quebec.

My hon. friend would
be right in his contention that it is easier for the people of my county to get access to the farm at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere if there were in existence to-day the same communications that were maintained in years past by the Canada Steamship Lines and also by the ferry from Riviere Ouelle to Murray Bay. But those two services have been discontinued, and the farmer in that district who wishes to go from Murray Bay to Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere will now have to go a long way around. He will have to go down as far as Tadoussac and take the ferry boat, a distance of over twenty miles, cross the river St. Lawrence or else take the train on the Quebec and Saguenay railway, go up to Quebec and then cross over the river and go the whole way round on the south shore of the St. Lawrence before he reaches Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere-or as an hon. gentleman suggests, swim across, because there is no ferry boat service. With the farm at Cap Rouge, and the activities all being carried on there as they were in the past, it would be much more convenient and easier of access and to the greatest advantage of the people of that district of Quebec. _

When I asked the minister how the $833,000 was made up he gave his answer rather hurriedly, and I was not able to take down the figures. I noticed however there was a considerable cut for

illustration stations. I should like to ask the Prime Minister, in view of a press report I saw some time ago to the effect that the government had bought and taken over the Seager Wheeler farm at Rosthem, what price was paid, and also whether it is going to be operated by the same help as is operating the experimental farm at Rosthem to-day. Will the same superintendent be in charge?

With reference to the Seager Wheeler farm, I would say that we have not paid anything for it, we have not bought it or we have not rented it. We have however established the position of experimental substation superintendent for Doctor Seager Wheeler. He will operate the farm as he has done in the past, continuing to carry out the experiments in which he has engaged so successfully. He has experimented not only in connection with grains and grasses, but also with fruits. At great sacrifice of his own time he has been an inspiration to many farmers and has been most unselfish in his advice to them. We felt no better investment could be made than to pay Seager Wheeler $2,220 per year as superintendent of a subexperimental station to assist him, now when he is getting up in years, to hire the necessary labour, so that he may have more time at his disposal to advise and assist the farmers in their experiments.
Outside of the gratuity given to Seager Wheeler by the government, he bears all the expense of the operation of the farm? He pays the taxes, and other expenses?
Yes.
As the experimental farm at Lennoxville is in my county, I should like to know the curtailment of the grant in connection with it.
The total reduction on the Lennoxville farm is $9,335, or 18 per cent.

What branches of work
are to be curtailed?

The salary reduction takes care of part of the decrease. So far as actual experimental activities are concerned, there will be no curtailment. We have decided it is not advisable in connection with the Lennoxville and various other experimental farms to try to carry on special breeding or genetical work with more than one breed of cows or other animals. In that way

Supply-Agriculture
we are saving considerable money by moving animals from one farm to another, and eliminating duplication.
I should like to ask if the same staff which was in charge 1930, at St. Joachim is still the same, or has there been any change since that time?
The same staff is there. It is under the supervision of the superintendent at Cap Rouge.

I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to the farm at Lacombe, Alberta. How much was spent last year and what will be spent this year? Although the farm is not in my riding, being in the constituency of Wetaskiwin, it is near my home, and I have made many pilgrimages to the place and have taken a good deal of interest in it. I have always felt they were doing all they possibly could with the money at their disposal. In what way could expenditures be curtailed on that farm without reducing the service they are giving?

In the year 1931-32 there was expended $50,984; the estimate for this year is $42,500, or a reduction of $8,484. Some of this reduction is because of the reduced salaries, and a further reduction is made by a change of policy in regard to live stock on the farm. That is, we are reducing our stock to certain breeds of one type. Prior to this year a farm was rented in conjunction with the work at Lacombe. The farm has been sold and for that reason we have found it necessary to a certain extent to curtail the work.

If the farm is sold there is no possibility of its being purchased by the government to form part of the experimental
station?
No.

Can the minister tell us the locations of the five farms mentioned by the hon. member for Dorchester? I know of the ones at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, Lennox-ville, and Cap Rouge, I do not know where the others are situated.

Farnham and
L'Assomption.
When were those farms established?
Farnham in 1922 and L'Assomption in 1927.
When were the other farms established?
Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere in 1911, La Feme in 1916 and Lennoxville in 1912.

What activities are
carried on at Farnham and L'Assomption?
Tobacco growing.
The other farms are used for general mixed farming?
Yes.
Were there any other farms established under the new administration?
No, not in the province of Quebec.
Is it the intention of the government to establish any new farms, other than those at present in existence?
The intention of the government will be made known when any new farms are established.
Have demonstration plots in the province of Quebec been reduced?
There is a reduction of seven.
Throughout the whole province?
Yes.
Is it true that the sixth farm mentioned by the hon. member for Dorchester, namely that at La Ferme, was closed?

Activities have been curtailed to a certain extent because the department did not feel the farm was well situated. It was in a low lying place, and the soil was not typical of the surrounding country.

Does the minister realize that in new districts, such as La Ferme, farms are very necessary? It would be most unfortunate if this farm was closed. These days we are hearing a great deal of talk about a back to the farm movement, and most of the talking is done, of course, by those who know nothing about farming. The first back to the land movement was initiated during the last election campaign. But since the members who were elected with this flag have resumed their ordinary urban occupations, they do not care any more about the back to the land movement. There is no minister for whom I have greater sympathy than the Minister of Agriculture, because he entered on the ad-
Supply-Agriculture

ministration of his department burdened by the many great promises made by his chief, and in his endeavour to redeem those promises I fully realize he may well be called the busy bee of the ministry, for I know he is overworking himself. But not only has he many great promises to redeem, he is further handicapped by his estimates being reduced one-third. I am sure he will agree with me that what is most needed to-day is not a back to the land movement, but a colonization movement. Colonization presents many difficult problems that the ordinary farmer is unable to solve, and I hope the minister will take into consideration the establishment of a new farm to be devoted especially to the solution of colonization problems, especially in the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, before this item is passed I thank the minister for not having curtailed his appropriation for the Lennoxville experimental farm. I also want to thank him and the officers of his department for the cooperation they have given, through the farm at Lennoxville-the finest experimental farm in all Canada-to the whole farming section of the eastern townships. But I do offer this criticism. If there is one thing that can help us back to prosperity it is to increase the purchasing power of the agricultural classes. When I consider the curtailment of the minister's estimates I realize he has had a very hard job in retaining them even at their present figure, but I think he should put up a still harder fight. There is no excuse whatever for cutting the agricultural estimates by over $3,200,000 odd. I do not criticize the curtailment of the appropriations for certain branches in connection with the different experimental farms, but we should at least maintain the estimates for agriculture at their last year's figure, without of course undertaking new buildings and similar expenditures. I follow very closely the work at the Lennoxville experimental farm, and no doubt the committee will be interested to learn that last year, on Farmers' day, 1,500 farmers from all over the eastern townships attended a picnic at the farm. That is the largest meeting of agriculturists that has ever been held in any section of the eastern townships. It was not a political gathering; the farmers present were trying to better, if not increase, agricultural production. I repeat, the only criticism I have to offer is that the minister should not have reduced his estimates at all, but should have maintained them at least up to the standard of last year.

Mr. Chairman, as
I am responsible for the estimates in my department, I was confronted with this question: Could we in. view of present conditions, or even if these conditions did not exist, make any cut in the agriculture estimates without affecting detrimentally our agricultural interests? Personally I think that this cut will have practically no effect at all so far as efficiency in the department goes.

Has the minister an
itemized account showing the reductions that he proposes to make in the expenditures on the various experimental farms? I notice my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) thanked the minister for the kind manner in which he had treated the Lennoxville experimental farm. Naturally I am interested in our experimental farms, because I have one right in the middle of my own constituency. I should like to know to what extent the minister proposes to cut down that appropriation.

While we are not discussing the item of dairying at the moment, Mr. Chairman, yet we are dealing with the agriculture estimates. Therefore I wish to pay tribute to a gentleman who has been in the service of the government for a period of over forty years, and as he comes from the vicinity of my home I thought possibly it would be fitting on my part to give the committee a short account of his career. I refer to Doctor J. A. Ruddick, Dominion dairy commissioner.
He was born near Dorchester in Oxford county, Ontario, in 1862. As a young man he learned to make cheese and was engaged as a cheesemaker by the late D. M. Mac-Pherson of Lancaster, Ontario, who owned and operated some sixty cheese factories located in eastern Ontario and Quebec. After one year in charge of a factory Mr. Ruddick was engaged as superintendent of the combination.
Following the appointment in 1890 of the late James W. Robertson as Dominion dairy commissioner, Mr. Ruddick was in the spring of 1891 appointed to the dairy commissioner's staff and this was the first appointment to the staff. Mr. Ruddick as a member of the staff of the dairy commissioner carried on experimental work in the use of the Babcock milk test as a basis of division of factory proceeds, operated winter creameries in eastern and western Ontario for demonstration purposes, and in 1892 supervised the manufacture of the mammoth cheese for the world's fair, which cheese weighed eleven tons. He assisted in the organization and management of

Supply-Agriculture
creameries in the Northwest Territories and later became superintendent of the Eastern Dairy School, Kingston, Ontario. About 1898 he entered the service of the New Zealand government as first director of dairying in that dominion and remained in New Zealand for about eighteen months. He returned to Canada about 1900 and again joined the staff of the Dominion dairy commissioner. In 1900 he organized the work of cargo inspection at Montreal, which service is designed to ensure proper handling of perishable produce intended for export. In 1902 under the direction of Mr. Ruddick central cool cheese curing rooms were established at Woodstock, Brock ville, Oowansville and St. Hyacinthe for the purpose of demonstrating the benefits to be derived from the proper curing of cheese. During the latter part of 1901 James W. Robertson resigned as dairy commissioner and Mr. Ruddick was made Dominion dairy commissioner. During the great war he acted as a member of the cheese commission, set up to purchase and export Canada's surplus cheese. In 1918 the name of this commission was changed to the Dairy Produce Commission and it handled surplus butter and condensed milk as well as cheese. In 1921 the milk utilization service of the dairy and cold storage branch was organized. This service is designed to promote the domestic consumption of milk and milk products. In 1923 the grading by federal officers of butter and cheese for export became compulsory and the grading service was organized under Mr. Ruddick's direction. The same year the division of dairy research was established, the object of which is to determine causes of defects in cheese and butter and to suggest remedies.
In 1924, Mr. Ruddick was given the honorary degree of LL.D. by Queen's university of Kingston, Ontario.
I regret very much that Doctor Ruddick has arrived at the age of seventy years when he is supposed to retire from his duties. I am sure the Dominion of Canada will lose the services of an honourable, faithful and efficient servant in the person of Doctor Ruddick.

What is the amount of
the reduction, if any, in connection with the Kapuskasing experimental farm?

First, in reply to
my hon. friend from South Battleford, so that he will not worry unduly, the vote last year was $46,145 for the experimental farm about which he asked. The vote this year is $40,000, so the reduction amounts to S6,145, the greater part of which is a salary reduction.
With reference to Kapuskasing, last year the vote was $48,045; this year the estimate is $41,000, a reduction of $7,045.

What activities will be
particularly curtailed?

The chief reduction
is in salaries. Land improvement work will be curtailed and there will be some reduction in the live stock division.

I really believe the land improvement work could be dropped for the time being, but I want to protest as strongly as possible against any curtailment of work in connection with live stock. We in northern Ontario hear on many occasions of the wonderful things that are being done for the western farmers. We do not begrudge them anything, but northern Ontario is a new and rich agricultural section of the country. It is in what we call a clay belt, and instead of being curtailed the live stock activities should be increased for the very good reason that many of our farmers cannot afford to go to southern Ontario, Quebec, or the western provinces for the stock they require. I think the full activity of this branch should be maintained. I speak feelingly on this matter, because while I was on the government side of the house I asked every year for an increase in the amount voted for the Kapuskasing experimental farm, and I was to some extent successful. I think this is not the right time to curtail the amoimt spent in that way. I fully realize the situation in which the minister now finds himself, but I hope he will be able at least to maintain the live stock activities carried on at the Kapuskasing experimental farm. I do not wTant to say more on this subject, because I have spoken on the matter previously.
There is another question I should like to ask the minister, and in this connection I should like to give all credit to the province of Ontario. Last fall they threatened to close the Hearst demonstration farm, but we are glad to learn that they are not going to do so. I understand, however, that the federal government has built a dwelling house at Kapuskasing for the superintendent of the Hearst demonstration farm. We know that this gentleman, who is exceptionally well qualified for his work, should live in the town of Hearst, and the settlers of that district do not want to see the head of that demonstration farm moved to Kapuskasing. Experimental farms come under the jurisdiction of the federal government, while demonstration farms come under provincial jurisdiction. It has been brought to my notice
Supply-Agriculture

that a certain amount of money has been spent by this government for the construction of a house for the superintendent of the Hearst demonstration farm, and I should like to know from the minister if that information is correct.

I may tell my hon. friend that the reduction is in the number of cattle. We decided, for the very reason the hon. gentleman has in mind, that we must give all the assistance possible in these new areas, but we felt that we would do more in that way by disposing of the grade cattle and increasing the number of pure bred cattle so there would be more seed stock available in that new country. With regard to the closing of the Hearst demonstration farm, which is a provincial farm, as I stated at the outset this action was taken in accordance with the policy of cooperation between the federal department of agriculture and the provincial department. It was felt that the money expended on the Hearst farm could be better used in further assistance to farmers in northern Ontario and that the work could be well carried on, as far as attacking agricultural problems was concerned, at the Kapuskasing farm. I did not catch the last question of the hon. member.

I have received a number of letters to the effect that the federal government spent a certain amount of money in the construction of a dwelling house for Mr. Hanlan, a friend of mine of the north country, the superintendent of the Hearst demonstration farm. The people in Hearst, who expected the demonstration farm to be maintained, believed Mr. Hanlan should remain in Hearst so that there might not be any conflict between the activities of the two governments. It will be hard to explain why a provincial official should come under federal jurisdiction, and why his activities should be curtailed to a certain extent.

His activities will
not be curtailed. It was felt that it would be better for him to live on the farm where the experiments were being conducted, so a cottage was built at a cost of about $3,100. So long as he makes that cottage his headquarters my understanding is that he will continue to occupy it.

We were under the
impression that the Hearst demonstration farm was to be maintained by the provincial government. The statement appeared in the press that activities at that farm were not

to be curtailed, and if that is to be the case it seems strange that the superintendent should reside at the Kapuskasing farm.

The Hearst farm is a provincial farm, but in conference we agreed that it would cut out waste, without removing any great benefit from agriculture, if the provincial government should close that farm and have that money available for other purposes. It was agreed that Mr. Hanlan, who is now residing on the Kapuskasing farm, should make that his headquarters.

Then I understand that by arrangement between the two governments the demonstration farm has been closed. I think that is a bad move, because I maintain that the provincial government should have continued to operate the demonstration farm at Hearst. In northern Ontario we need to have all the agricultural experiments that we can get the benefit of, and the activities carried on at the Hearst demonstration farm were doing a great deal of good. This farm is at least seventy-five miles from the Kapuskasing farm, and it dealt with matters that were not taken up at Kapuskasing. If it is at all possible I think the federal authorities should tell the provincial authorities that the Hearst farm should be maintained and that Mr. Hanlan, a very able agriculturist, should be sent back to Hearst. He might extend his activities to Kapuskasing or other portions of northern Ontario if possible, but he should be located at Hearst, and I hope the minister will use his influence to bring about that result. The province of Ontario should be able to maintain that farm without asking the help of the federal government, or at least without discontinuing its needed services at Hearst.

I gather that the
Hearst farm is in the constituency represented by the hon. member. There is no gain, so far as experimental work goes, in having a farm at Hearst, because soil and other conditions are almost identical at Kapuskasing. With regard to the Ontario department of agriculture, we have spent a great deal of time in bringing about cooperation in attacking agricultural problems of an experimental or research nature, and it was agreed after full consideration that there was no advantage in operating the two farms.

I want to thank the
minister for his explanation. He said something about the experimental farm at La Ferme, pointing out that the soil was not of such a quality as warranted the continuation

Supply-Agriculture
of great activities there. I happen, to know something about the constituency so well represented by the hon. member for Pontiac. The statement that the soil is low is not quite right; it is fairly high and fairly hilly. Has the minister in mind some other site for an experimental farm in northern Quebec? This is important. Although I do not belong to the province of Quebec, I am interested in the northern section of Canada and its agricultural development, and I am fully convinced, from the series of experiments we have carried out at Kapuskasing and La Ferme, that the possibility has been demonstrated of extensive colonization in that district. Does the department intend to choose another site? I said that the land was not altogether low; it is not typical of the clay belt, but it also has some good farming features. Did the minister have in view another site on which enormous sums would be spent before it could become an experimental farm? I thought it would be wise to maintain activities for a few years instead of curtailing them on that farm.
Is it the policy of the experimental farms to sell their surplus products?
Yes.

This being so, I wish to lodge a complaint with the minister on behalf of the honey producers of British Columbia. In their search for a market they were told by the wholesalers that they would have to accept 2 cents less per pound owing to the fact that the experimental farm had sold honey at a lower price. If we have surplus products from our experimental farms, surely the penitentiaries and other government institutions could take them. It is very unfair to our producers in British Columbia for them to have to compete with the experimental farms. We have to meet competition from the rest of the world, particularly from the east, and our situation is aggravated when the honey producers have to compete with an experimental farm that has the dominion behind it. I hope the minister will take this matter into serious consideration and in future prohibit such competition in the open market with our producers.

No doubt the instance cited by the hon. gentleman is correct. It certainly is not the policy of the farms to compete with private producers by underselling them. My information is that they sell to the wholesalers at prevailing prices, and as a matter of fact we have had a good deal 41701-195
of criticism by reason of the high prices charged by the experimental farms. I shall be glad to take the matter into consideration.
The complaint was made to me on behalf of the honey producers of the province.

Mr. Chairman, may I submit to the committee the correspondence exchanged between the hon. Adelard Godbout, Minister of Agriculture for the province of Quebec, and myself. This correspondence refers to the distribution of seed grain in Quebec. On May 10, last, I wrote the following letter to the hon. Mr. Godbout:
Hon. Mr. Adelard Godbout,
Minister of Agriculture,
Quebec.
Dear Mr. Godbout,-
Mr. Emiliano Simoneau, farmer, of Windsor Mills, informs me that he will be unable to sow his land this year. He has not the funds necessary to purchase seed grain.
Mr. Simoneau is an excellent farmer who is much attached to his land, he would be thankful to receive government assistance. This gentleman is desirous of securing 100 pounds of millet, 100 pounds of medium red clover, 25 bushels of oats and 10 bushels of barley. If you could possibly assist Mr. Simoneau, he would greatly appreciate it.
Yours faithfully,
F. J. Lafleche, M.P.
The following is the Hon. Mr. Godbout's answer:
Department of Agriculture Province of Quebec Office of the Minister.
Quebec, May 16, 1932. Mr. F. J. Lafleche, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-
I am in receipt of your confidential letter, dated the 10th inst. and in which you request assistance from the provincial government on behalf of Mr. Emiliano Simoneau, farmer, of Windsor Mills, in order to enable him to secure seed grain.
The provincial government in fact, distributes seed grain to farmers in need in the poorest parts of the province. This distribution is carried out through the medium of parish committees presided by the local parish priest, the members of these local committees are, in fact, better able to judge of the needs of each person.
The amount set aside by the provincial government, this year, to assist the farming class in purchasing seed grain for those w'ho most need it, is still larger than last year.
For your own information, allow me to point out to you that we have again requested, from the Dominion government this year, assistance for the Quebec farmers, just as they do for other provinces; unfortunately we have not been able to obtain anything, no more than we were able last year.

309S
Supply-Agriculture

May I further state, for your information also, that we were informed last year that the Dominion Unemployment and Farm Relief Act could not be so interpreted as to apply the money for the relief of those in need, to purchasing seed grain.
You will readily understand that, under these circumstances, it is impossible for us to do more. Indeed, although it may not seem very large for each parish, the contribution of the Quebec government, alone, this year, amounts to a much larger sum owing to the great number of parishes of the province, where we are obliged to contribute, and this, notwithstanding that money is scarcer this year. We requested the government, at Ottawa, to contribute an amount equal to the one we, ourselves, apply to these purchases of seed grain; if the Dominion government had consented, at least, to contribute a portion, even had it been only half of what we appropriate for that end, or again if the government, at Ottawa, had but guaranteed the amount required, I think that we would have probably been able to distribute to all farmers that were in need, in Quebec, the quantity of seed grain they required.
It is unfortunate, indeed, that the Dominion Act in this respect does not equally apply to all the provinces.
May I assure you of my best endeavours, Yours faithfully,
Adelard Oodbout.
I should like to inquire from the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), whether it is a fact that the Quebec provincial government has made such a request and whether the Dominion government refused to consider it.
This question interests particularly the Quebec farmers, since the press siding with the opposition contend that the Dominion government grants all the requests coming from the western provinces and refuses those from Quebec. The Minister of Agriculture of Quebec has written to the local member of the county of Wolfe a similar letter as the one addressed to me.
It is important to know definitely whether the statement of the Minister of Agriculture for Quebec is founded on fact or not. I therefore beg the hon. Minister of Agriculture to inform the committee in this respect.

The hon. member
for Richmond-Wolfe signified his intention of asking this question with reference to assistance from the federal government to the farmers in the purchasing of seed grain in the province of Quebec. On May 2 I received the following telegram from the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec:
Hon. Robert Weir,
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Ontario.
An inquiry reveals that a very great number of farmers and settlers are absolutely unable to secure their seeds this spring. The Quebec

government has already granted $200,000 to answer the most urgent requirements but we realize that it is insufficient and that another $200,000 will be necessary to meet the situation. We hope that the federal government could supply that additional amount. Letter follows.
Adelard Godbout,
Minister of Agriculture.
On May 5 I replied to the Minister of Agriculture for Quebec in this letter:
Ottawa, May 5, 1932.
Hon. A. Godbout,
Minister of Agriculture,
Quebec, Que.
Dear Mr. Godbout:
I asknowledge receipt of your telegram of the 2nd instant, reading as follows:
An inquiry reveals that a very great number of farmers and settlers are absolutely unable to secure their seeds this spring. The Quebec government has already granted $200,000 to answer the most urgent requirements but we realize that it is insufficient and that another $200,000 will be necessary to meet the situation. We hope that the federal government could supply that additional amount. Letter follows.
And also your letter of the 3rd instant. We have no authority or appropriation to provide for the purchase or distribution of seed in any province and, therefore, I am unable to comply with the request which you have made.
In case you have been misinformed with regard to the situation, I might say that we are not purchasing or distributing seed grain for any province as this is considered to be a provincial responsibility entirely.
I believe the letter from Mr. Godbout to the hon. member for Richmondt-Wolfe was written on May 16, at least ten days later. I have endeavoured on different occasions to make this point as dear as possible: the federal. government has not purchased seed for any farmer in any province of the Dominion of Canada. If for any reason the provincial governments felt that they could not carry on the services of government and have submitted that -condition of affairs to the federal government, the matter has been given full consideration and money has been loaned to the provincial governments when the federal government felt that the, demands were warranted. I do not know that I can make this point any clearer than that. I have made that statement before in the house more than once, and I regret that Mr. Godbout evidently did not understand my letter, although I do not know how I could have made it any clearer than in the language I used. The government of Quebec has not made any request to the federal government for a loan to help to carry on the services of government and look after their farmers in connection with seed grain or other matters. If they had, no reasonable person would suggest for a minute that they would not be

treated the same as the other provinces. I do nob think there is anything I can add in respect to this matter.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to protest against the remarks just made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture. In order that the Quebec farmers be granted assistance by the Dominion Minister of Agriculture, the latter insists that, as an essential condition, the government of that province should prove that it is so financially embarrassed, that it is unable to provide for its own agricultural requirements.
Exactly like in all other provinces.

What the . Quebec Minister of Agriculture requested the dominion government to do, was that the government or the Department of Agriculture should grant the Quebec farmers an amount equal to the one contributed by the provincial Department of Agriculture. I think, it is only fair, especially, when we are aware of the fact that if the Minister of Agriculture occupies his present position, it is due to the numerous pledges made to the Quebec farmers. They were promised, among other things that they would be assisted in all their requirements. There is no better time to do so than now. This government has now been in power for two years and has done nothing to help the Quebec farmers. The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) for whom I have much regard-he is aware of it-
He deserves some.

-stated, a moment ago, in the course of this debate, that the impression should not spread in Quebec that the government grants nothing to this province and all to the western provinces. It is not only an impression-we are facing a fact-and I am quite convinced that the Quebec members, whether they belong to the Liberal or Conservative party, if they wish to be impartial, will necessarily come to the conclusion that the Minister of Agriculture has done nothing to help the Quebec farmers.

May I ask the hon. member a question?
Some hon. MEMBERS (Translation): Order!

And when the provincial Minister of Agriculture asks the dominion minister to co-operate and requests him to grant to our farmers a similar 41761-195J
amount to that granted by the provincial government, in order to assist the farmers in purchasing seed grain, the only reply from the minister, is that the dominion government gives no seed grain to any province; if any province wishes to secure seed grain, that province-I repeat what I stated at the outset-it must be so financially embarrassed that it is unable to provide for their own agricultural requirements.
Not necessarily.

I wish to protest against the stand taken by the Minister of Agriculture. It is said, not only in Quebec but also in Ontario, that this government seems to grant its favours rather to the western farmers. I state that this impression is founded on facts. Last year, when the question of granting to western farmers a 5 cents rebate per bushel of wheat exported, came up, we requested the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. Minister of Agriculture to grant a similar rebate to those who, in Quebec and Ontario, were engaged in the dairy industry. This request was refused. On various occasions, this session, we again made the same request. In my comments on the budget, again I made the request to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture, that they grant to the Quebec farmers a similar amount to the one granted to the western farmers. When the government conceded this 5 cents rebate per bushel of wheat exported, they were not making a loan to the western provinces, but a gift. We ask the Minister of Agriculture to grant, this year, to Quebec the same amount which was given last year to the three western provinces. I think that this is a legitimate and fair proposition, and I cannot understand why the request made by the hon. Mr. Godbout-
There was never an official request made.

-was not granted by the dominion government.

the letters read by the Minister of Agriculture passing between himself and the Hon. Mr. Godbout, and it was apparent from the whole remarks of the hon. member that he had one object and one object alone in view and that was to sidetrack the question. The letter of Mr. Godbout to the hon. member for Rich-mond-Wolfe said in part:
It is indeed unfortunate that the federal law .n this respect does not apply in the same way 10 all the provinces of Canada.
That was the contention of the hon. Minister of Agriculture in the province of Quebec. The federal Minister of Agriculture in his answer made clear that the same law and the same treatment applied to everyone in Canada. Now what is the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska asking for? He is asking for special treatment for the province of Quebec; not that Quebec should be treated the same as the other provinces, as Mr. Godbout contended in his letter, but that Quebec should receive special treatment. He asks that the federal government at Ottawa should make a special grant to the province of Quebec for the purpose of buying seed grain, and so I say, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member is trying to sidetrack the question.
I can quite understand that the Quebec government would not dare to make application to this government for any aid for the citizens of the province of Quebec, for the very good reason that the Prime Minister of the province in his manifesto issued at St. Raymond, declared that there was no unemployment in the province of Quebec and that any there might be the government of the province of Quebec could very well take care of.
What has that to do with seed grain?

Well, if the situation in Quebec was so flourishing that there was no unemployment, and if the Quebec government could take care of any unemployment there might be without help from the federal government, I do not see how Mr. Godbout or Mr. Taschereau or the provincial government can now come to this government and ask for aid.
Mr. Ferguson said in 1930 that the Ontario government could take care of the unemployed in the province, and then later he lambasted the Dominion government because it did not assist.
I am not aware that the government of Ontario has applied to this government for seed grain.
You may not be aware of it, but we know it.

How can the Quebec government come here and ask for aid in view of their declarations? If they ask for aid they will receive at the hands of this government exactly the same treatment as every other province of Canada. But in view of the declarations the premier of the province made in his manifesto, and which have been repeated several times since, not only by himself but by every member of his cabinet, and in view of the amount that the provincial government allowed to be expended on the roads last year during the election campaign, I think it would be very hard for them to prove to this government that the province of Quebec was entitled to seed grain. But if they come to this government- and put before them the situation exactly as it is, I feel sure this government will grant them every aid and lend them money just the same as it has lent money to the western provinces. Perhaps the government of Quebec will come to this government and say: We owe to the citizens of the province of Quebec ten or eleven or twelve or thirteen -million dollars for work done on the roads of the province last year and not yet paid for. I trust the house realizes the situation in which our poor people of Quebec are placed. I do not know the exact figure, and I do not think -the provincial government itself knows, but it does owe approximately ten or twelve million dollars for work done on the roads last year. I know one parish in my county where the provincial government still owes $12,000 for work that was done, and in general fifty per cent of the work was useless. But the money was spent just the same ; the poor farmers of Quebec earned ithe money and as yet they have not received one dollar of it. I could' give you -the names of many municipalities in my constituency in which work was done for which the provincial government- owes money. So I say, Mr. Chairman, that if the Quebec government would put the facts as they are, not as they represent them to be, before this government, they would: receive just the same treatment as any other province. Mr. Taschereau claims that he is going to have another good surplus on the thirtieth of June. Very likely he will show a surplus, but the province will still be owing to its citizens between twelve and fifteen million dollars. I repeat, that if the Quebec government places before this government, the situation exactly as it is in the province of Quebec, I have no doubt that -the provincial government will receive its seed grain, because undoubtedly Quebec is in as bad a position as many of the other provinces.

But that is not all. Not only is money owed by the provincial government to farmers and settlers who have been working on the roads, but the provincial government also owes .practically all grants to schools, .practically all grants to farmers' clubs and practically all grants to agricultural societies of every kind. They have not made any payments since last year. Then I do not know how many hundreds of thousands of dollars is owing by the provincial government to its employees for salaries. One man told me personally that the provincial government owed him over one thousand dollars in salary. That is the situation with all their employees in the province of Quebec. I do not wish to delay the committee, Mr. Chairman, but I think these facts should be placed before it so that every member will realize the situation in which we are placed in the province of Quebec. _ _
There is just one other matter. The Minister of Agriculture this. afternoon was very charitable. He said he thought the Quebec Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Godbout, must have misinterpreted his letter. I disagree in that regard, because I believe Mr. Godbout understood perfectly the meaning of the letter. When he wrote the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe he knew he was not writing the truth. He knew that the statements in his letter were not according to facts. Although he is a new minister in the executive council' of the province of Quebec, and although we may say he is a new politician, he has learned the game very quickly.
They do in Quebec.

They certainly do. He has followed the example of the rest of the council. Politics is the first thing they think about; it is ahead of everything. Politicians in that province think first of the party; then if the interests of the citizens do no't conflict with party interests the citizens are given some consideration. The fact is, however, that every day of the year they are sacrificing the interests of the citizens of the province of Quebec, because they are not in accordance with the interests of the Liberal party.
I conclude by saying that Mr. Godbout was not sincere at all. I have no doubt he sent a similar letter to many other people, in an effort to deceive the population of the province of Quebec. He is trying to put a load on the federal government which they themselves cannot carry. That is his intention, and that is -what he has been doing.

Mr. Chairman, I was just

I do know, however-and I think the hon. member for Compton does not know it-that this government owes something to the province of Quebec. My hon. friend's leader promised in 1930 that he would put every man to work, or perish in the attempt.
Cheap.

The province of Quebec has
been forced to proceed with its plan of road work because of the failure of this government to carry out its promises.

speechtext: Probably I had better answer that question. The Dominion of Canada offered to lend money to any province desiring to purchase seed grain for its people. It loaned money; it did not give it. The provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta secured loans for that purpose, for which they gave their treasury bills or notes payable with interest. They made the arrangements with their own people as to the terms on which they loaned the money to them or bought the seed grain for them.

speechtext:
Yes; I speak subject to
correction. In order to assist last fall Mr. McFarland took some preliminary steps to secure seed grain, which was subsequently bought by the province and distributed to the population, for which I understand under the provisions of a statute they gave notes secured by liens against the crops which will be grown with the seed. The terms and conditions under which the money was expended for seed, and the conditions under which the settlers received the seed, are wholly within the power of the provinces, and they made their own arrangements.

Suppose the farmers
do not give any security for their notes, and suppose that times continue to be bad, the notes will not be paid, and then the provinces will turn round and say to the federal government:	We have not been able to collect on
our notes, and therefore we are not going to pay our loan. Then eventually the loan will be written off. This is the money of the whole Canadian people to which the people of my province are contributing; and in that way they are contributing for the purchasing of seed grain in some sections of Canada while at the same time they are not receiving the same benefits.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is talk just such as
that which brings public men into disrepute. The hon. gentleman is a past master at that sort of thing; that seems to be his one job, to endeavour to stir up animosity between provinces or between peoples. He knows perfectly well that the money loaned by this dominion to the provinces was secured by the treasury bills or bonds which they gave for the loans. He knows further-as every hon. gentleman knows-that the provinces made their own arrangements with respect to the purchase and distribution of seed grain, and took a loan upon the crop to be grown therefrom. To suggest that these men would repudiate their obligations or endeavour to escape the debts which were created does scant justice to the hardy pioneer spirit which they have shown. The other day a gentleman who had just come back from the west told me that the only optimists he had discovered were the men who are doing just what these men are doing. I cannot but deprecate-and I think every fair-minded man deprecates-this attempt to have it appear that Quebec is paying money for seed grain in Saskatchewan, and that possibly it will be lost money, a bad debt, and will have to be written off. If the province of Quebec desires to take a loan from this dominion for the purpose of providing its settlers with seed grain, that is available to-morrow. What is more, that is well known, too. I have seen the circulars that have been sent about by some members from Quebec for the purpose of endeavouring to have it appear that this government is favouring the three western provinces at the expense of the people of Quebec. I am bound to say that decent-minded people resent that kind of thing. There is no part of this country more willing to make its contribution to the national wellbeing than Quebec, and the hon. member does not interpret the genius of those people in their attitude towards the other provinces.
What the Prime Minister deprecates so strongly now was part of the campaign of the Tory party in 1930.
Very cheap.
When party feeling has subsided-
It has not.
-may I ask the Minister of Agriculture to tell me what was the character of the work carried on at the Morrin rock farm substation, or whatever they call it?
The chief work was a study, under the entomological branch, of the western cut-worm.
They were also carrying on some investigation into the wire-worm ?
Yes.
Is that work to be continued or has it been curtailed?
I understand it has not been curtailed; it will be continued.

I have not heard
any discussion with regard to the illustration stations which come under this item, except as to the extent to which the item has been reduced. I think $17,555 apportioned for the illustration stations has been reduced. I would commend to the minister the work of these small illustration stations-at least as I know them. It so happens that in the province of Saskatchewan we have just four experimental farms. Obviously they are very far removed from each other, and it is impossible for the people in general to get in touch with them. In my own constituency I happen to have two of these small illustration stations, and I can say in regard to one of them that it is doing a splendid work in a small way at a minimum of expense. I think I am correct in saying that the total expenditure in connection with that one illustration station is about $250, possibly less, and yet it serves a community within a radius of twenty-five or thirty-five miles. I have figures showing that the expenditure in connection with some of the experimental farms amounts to over $40,000 each. Therefore one hundred and sixty of these little illustration stations could be run at the same expenditure as is necessary for one of the large farms. I am quite sure what they would accomplish would be comparatively more than what is accomplished by the large farms.
I do not know whether the minister is curtailing the work of those illustration stations or closing some of them out, or whether he is just decreasing the amount of money expended on each, but I would bespeak his favourable consideration for them. The large farms operating in Saskatchewan are located on a type of soil that is qute different from the soil in some other districts, and that is where the small stations can perform a very useful work. The one in my own district is close to the town in which I reside and is located on a heavy type of soil. We are fortunate in having a good practical farmer to supervise that station. He keeps everv-
Supply-Agriculture

thing in good shape. The farm is located on a well-travelled provincial highway, and is open for the inspection of the public at any time they go by. Every fall the supervisor has a field day- when some two or three speakers are brought in either from the Scott or Swift Current experimental farms and a general assemblage of the farmers of the district is held under the auspices of the Kinders-ley Agricultural Society. I have been privileged to attend a number of those field days, and they impressed me very favourably. Considering the small expenditure made, the number of people that take advantage of those gatherings would indicate that the benefits to the local farmers are more than one might expect. Possibly from seventy-five to a hundred farmers assemble for the afternoon to listen to the addresses and inspect the different crops on the illustration station. They also get information with regard to different kinds of grain and grass seeds, and so on. Therefore I would say that having regard to the expenditure involved the work done by these small illustration stations is of considerable advantage to the farmers in the locality and should be continued. So far as Saskatchewan is concerned, have any of the illustration stations been closed?
Three have been recently closed.
How many are still in operation?
Twenty-eight.

I think last
year a two hundred and fifty acre farm was purchased near Regina for experimental purposes. What is being done with the land?

It was suggested
that we purchase an experimental farm in that heavy clay ground, but it was felt we could achieve the purpose and deal with the problem that they wished dealt with much more cheaply by renting a half-section. The work carried on is the study of weeds and especially of soil conditions, and the work is being continued.

Mr. W'EIR (Melfort): There is Kapuskasing in the north and Harrow in the southwest.
That would make three, the one at Ottawa and the two the minister has just mentioned?

Mr. WrEIR (Melfort): The reduction in the substations is $16,000, and the reduction in the central experimental farm is $106,402. I would like to know if the three illustration stations in the southern part of Saskatchewan, at Agema, at Rockglen and at Gravelburg, will be kept in operation this year.

They are still in
operation.

Mr. W'EIR (Melfort): In all there have been three recently closed. Is the station at Churchbridge in my hon. friend's constituency?

No, I do not know where that is. I think before the last government went out of office there was an investigation made into the possibility of opening an illustration station in the northwestern part of the riding of North Battleford, north of the Beaver river. I asked for and received a parliamentary return last session in that regard, and the decision at the time was that establishment of the station in question could not be entertained. I am sure the minister will agree with me that during the last two years a great many farmers have gone into that part of the north from the southern and central parts of Saskatchewan, and because of this, that area is now fully settled. I believe the time is at hand when the people in that northern area would be very grateful to the minister if he would take up that question again and do what he can to open an illustration station there to guide and help the farmers in the development of that splendid territory.
Wkile I am on my feet I want to thank the minister for what he has done in opening

a new illustration station at Hafford, on the Canadian National railway between North Battleford and Prince Albert. I am not sure whether or not that station is in operation, but I know it was intended to have it going this year.
It is in operation.
Thank you.

Just a few minutes
before recess I understood the minister to say that his department contemplated the closing of the experimental farm at La Perme, in the Abitibi district of northern Quebec. I strongly urge the department that this farm be continued, because of the peculiar situation which exists in that part of the country. This is a new country which has been opened to agriculture for only perhaps fifteen or twenty years. The people have gone there with that pioneer spirit upon which the Prime Minister is so prone to expatiate in this house. It seems to me that by closing down the experimental farm at that point the department would do a very poor service for those pioneers, those new settlers, those brave and worthy Canadians who are trying their best to open up a new district. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will take the case of these pioneers into his very serious consideration and not close down the experimental station at this point.

Mr. Chairman, the discussion seems to have wandered rather far from the item before the committee, and if I may I am going to direct a question to the minister which is not directly associated with the item now under discussion.
On different occasions in the house mention has been made of a marketing board; something has been said in favour of such an organization and something has been said against it. The county which I represent, so far as it is engaged in agriculture, is largely devoted to dairying and is deeply interested in butter, which is selling at a very low price. Whether or not a marketing board would prove successful in coming to the rescue of the beef producers or the wheat growers 1 do not know. It seems to me that the useful service which might be rendered by a marketing board depends to a very great extent on what proportion of the commodity produced is available for export, because it is the portion which goes into the markets of the world that determines the price at home. We are told that the consumption of butter in Canada has decreased materially due to hard times. We are told that last year we produced about
280.000.	000 pounds of butter and that this amount, less than about 3 per cent or from
10.000.	000 to 11,000,000 pounds, was consumed in Canada. The rest was exported, and the price of that small portion which was exported has fixed and determined the price of that which was sold in the country. As someone put it, if we produced 100 boxes of butter and shipped one box. the price at which we could sell the one box determined the price of the remainder. If it be true that we have but this small surplus to export, and we are exporting it to countries whose currency is depreciated, and as a consequence we are obliged to accept a price which is not only low in the face value of that currency, but lower still when it is transferred into our own currency, might we not do something for this industry by applying to our butter industry what other countries similarly situated have done? One-half of one cent levied on each pound of creamery butter produced in Canada last year, estimating the production to have been about 200,000,000 pounds, would have given $100,000, which would have been sufficient to raise the price of our export butter 5 or 6 cents a pound. And if it is the price of export butter-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would direct your attention to item 39, which is dairying.
The hon. gentleman is right. This discussion is absolutely out of order. If hon. members are to return to the marketing board we shall never get through the estimates.
It was discussed all afternoon yesterday.
That is quite true, but we have talked about everything under the item expect butter, and my suggestion was merely this-
May I ask for your ruling on the point of order, Mr. Chairman?
I must uphold the point of order; the present discussion is out -of order. The committee is now considering experimental farms.

Not yet. I do not think I should allow this vote to go by without expressing some of my disappointment at the emasculated condition it was in when it first came down. Earlier in the session I was capable of being shocked, and in fact I was shocked when I first saw the

vote; but I have had so many shocks since then that my shock-absorber has reached the saturation point, and I have ceased to be shocked any more. Besides that, I am somewhat mollified by the supplementary estimates, at least to the extent of about six per cent. There has been some reparation, especially in connection with this vote for experimental farms, so that the government has come back to normal to the extent of six per cent. I am not going to blame the minister very much. I have been in his shoes so many times and so long that I know he did not bring down the estimates to council in this dismantled form in the first instance. I am sure that his director, sitting in front of him, did not pass them on to his deputy in that reduced way in the first instance, nor the deputy to the minister, the minister to the treasury board, and the treasury board to council. There was a nigger in the woodpile somewhere else when these estimates were prepared, and I am wondering who it was. The then Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) has, of course, to sit hard on the chest; that is his duty. But if you have a good case-
I rise to a point of order also. The hon. gentleman is out of order, and it is to be regretted-

I am talking about this vote and the smallness of it, and I was going to give the minister a kindly tip how to avoid such disastrous reductions in the future. If the minister says that he does not want it, I will not give him the advice-
Oh, oh.

-but I am not going to heed the bowlings of the rear guard.
4n hon. MEMBER: He doesn't need your advice.
I needed it at one time, and I suspect the minister won't be any the worse for it. However, we will let it go and I will give it to him confidentially.
Carried.
No,.it is not carried. \ou don't like my tips over there. I wonder whether the minister would consider this-
I want a decision on my point of order.

There is no point of order about it. As I was saying, I want the minister to consider this. We have had various kinds of cuts this session-the Bennett cut, the Rhodes cut, and the cut on civil servants-

but this experimental farms cut is "the most unkindest cut of all," and I was wanting the minister to avoid it another year. We have been promised that the ten per cent cut in salaries and indemnities will be for one year only, and if the minister would assure us that he would endeavour to have his colleagues seriously consider making this reduction in connection with experimental farms and agriculture generally for one year only, trying to get back to normal next year, I would not say anything further. In fact. I would not say anything at all about any of the estimates because there is not much use doing so, pai

ticularly now the government have demonstrated in the supplementary estimates their recognition that they made a profound blunder in reducing agriculture in this way in the first instance. I want to express my appreciation of what the government has come to realize and admit this to be so, and I trust that the minister will endeavour to put agriculture in the same one-year category as the rest of us in regard to reductions. I am asking for agriculture only what has been granted to myself, namely, that this reduction as in the case of the members' ten per cent cut, will be for one year only. The Senate has got the same promise and so have the civil servants, and surely agriculture, which sustains us all and keeps half the people of Canada occupied, is worthy of the same consideration that is given members of the house and of the Senate. I do not even ask the minister for a reply; I simply ask him to take this suggestion into his very best reasoned consideration and work hard for its consummation next year.

I have just one question to ask the minister. I know that he realizes the mistake that he has made in connection with the estimates, and I have faith that he will play the game, in spite of what my friend has said. The minister knows quite well how important the tobacco industry in southern Ontario is, and what rapid strides it has made. He knows what it means to those farmers engaged in it. He knows what is being done in part of Oxford county, in Norfolk and Elgin, in experimentation and demonstration for the benefit of the farmers who are following along that line. Mr. Chairman I notice, by this item, that the government is carrying on its policy of cutting down expenditure. Last year the government appropriated for agricultural exhibitions the sum of $650,000. This year the grant is reduced to $350,000. It is a cut of $350,000 at 46 per cent. The assistance given to agricultural exhibitions represents outwardly, since it is a kind of advertisement, assistance to farming. The item therefore entirely sums up the government's policy. This year, the government under pretext of cutting down expenditure, thought fit to reduce the estimates of agriculture. Others who preceded me in this debate have stated their views on this kind of economy as vexatious as it is irrational. If there is a department where the estimates should have been increased instead of being cut down, it is certainly. that of agriculture.
It is common topic that agriculture is the foundation of the national economic structure. This house has often heard it repeated. It appears daily in the press. Economists are unanimous in proclaiming it. A nation without agriculture cannot subsist. History gives us many proofs of this. The world of to-day would not be undergoing such a serious crisis, if it had not forgotten that underlying principle. It is not only in the economic field that a chasm intervenes between the principle and the practice. But it is always amazing to note how easily under the sway of ambition, one neglects what would prove its strength and resistance, and how easily one forsakes the prey for the shadow.
The Canadian people have done so.

The shadow is overcapitalized industry, industry on a large scale. The prey is the land, the soil, agriculture. A number of countries such as England, Germany and Japan, owing to an overcrowded population from which they suffered had to forsake the land and go in for an intensive and unbounded industrial development. They depend on other countries for their living. And it is in the former countries that the crisis is most acute: it is industrial, financial, commercial, and therefor social in character.
Here, in Canada, there would be no reason to suffer from such depression, if we had strictly adhered to the principle that agriculture is the foundation of all lasting economic structure, if we had not despised this axiom,

a common-place one, so admitted by all. Canada encloses a vast area of land suited to farming but not yet settled. The land at our disposal is perhaps not unlimited as it was truly pointed out, it is, however, considerable, especially in Ontario and Quebec.
We are fortunately witnessing a change of thought which we would, however, like to see, more general. Some still imagine that when they have discussed trade, finances, currency, gold standard, transportation, they have covered all topics and feel quite at their ease.
They are laggards, they were responsible for the fiasco of our immigration policy and our deplorable emigration to the United States. Governments are still entangled in the webs of incoherent economic theories.
Broadminded people clearly saw the path to follow. They advocated settling the country and the back to the land movement in order to relieve congested cities and bring back the deserters to the farm.

What happened? There is some correspondence which might indicate differently, however, I attach no importance to it. On 'September 19, 1931, Mr. Jean writes again to the hon. Postmaster General-a long time after March 4, 1931. The deputy minister answers on September 28, 1931:
If it becomes necessary to make a change, the permanent appointment of the new incumbent will be made by the Civil Service Commission. The minister, however has taken your application under consideration.
Mention was made of permanent appointment. First, there was but a question of the appointment which was to be made by the Civil Service Commission. Finally, following inquiries held in the county of Temiscouata, by people with whom the minister is well acquainted, and whom I do not care to name, so as not to place them in the limelight, on February 5, 1932, a person by the name of Tardif, a blacksmith, was appointed. Was he appointed by the Civil Service Commission as the deputy minister wrote on March 4, 1931? No, he was appointed temporarily by the hon. Postmaster General who set aside the veteran.
I communicated with the commission on this matter to inquire why the vacancy was not advertised. I received the answer that the postmaster had not been dismissed after an inquiry had been held, but that he had been suspended, and that was the reason why the notice had not been posted. I wish to inquire from the hon. Postmaster General whether he intends to re-establish in his office, Jean-Baptiste Plourde, the former postmaster? I shall continue then .... Will the hon. Postmaster General inform me whether he has the intention to reinstate former postmaster?
